1	\section{Method}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\subsection{Task Formulation}
5	\label{sec:task}
6	
7	Given a text $x$, the goal is to predict its \emph{generation depth} $d \in \{0, 1, 2{+}\}$, where $d{=}0$ denotes human-written text, $d{=}1$ denotes first-generation LLM output conditioned on human text, and $d{=}2{+}$ denotes text produced by recursively conditioning an LLM on its own prior output at least twice.
8	Formally, let $\mathcal{C}_0$ be a reference corpus of human-written text.
9	A generation chain of depth $k$ is defined recursively: $x^{(0)} \sim \mathcal{C}_0$, and $x^{(k)} = G(x^{(k-1)})$ for $k \geq 1$, where $G$ denotes stochastic LLM generation conditioned on its input.
10	We frame depth estimation as an ordinal classification task over three classes rather than binary real-vs-synthetic detection, enabling finer-grained provenance characterization.
11	Depths beyond 2 are merged into a single $2{+}$ class, consistent with monotonic feature convergence that compresses inter-class margins beyond depth 2 (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
12	
13	\subsection{Generation Chain Construction}
14	\label{sec:generation}
15	
16	We construct generation chains using six generators spanning three model families: \textbf{Pythia} (2.8B, 1B) \cite{pythia}, \textbf{OLMo} (OLMo-2-1B) \cite{olmo}, and \textbf{Qwen} (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B-Base) \cite{qwen3}.
17	This selection covers parameter scales from 0.6B to 8.2B and diverse pretraining corpora, enabling evaluation of cross-generator and cross-scale generalization.
18	
19	For each generator, we sample approximately 1{,}000 seed passages from English Wikipedia as $\mathcal{C}_0$.
20	Each seed is iteratively fed through the generator to produce a chain of depth 4 (i.e., gen-0 through gen-4), using the prompt ``\texttt{Continue the following text: \{text\}}''.
21	All generation uses temperature $\tau{=}0.7$, nucleus sampling with $p{=}0.9$, and maximum length of 256 new tokens.
22	The resulting dataset contains approximately 27{,}000 texts across all generators and depths.
23	For classification, depths 2--4 are collapsed into the $2{+}$ class.
24	
25	\subsection{Feature Extraction}
26	\label{sec:features}
27	
28	The seven features are motivated by two complementary views of distributional drift.
29	Reference-model features capture how the text's token-level surprise distribution shifts relative to a fixed model; surface features capture how lexical diversity contracts under recursive generation.
30	Together, they span both the generative mechanism (what the model produces) and the surface manifestation (how the vocabulary changes).
31	This two-pronged design is not post-hoc: it follows directly from the hypothesis that recursive generation induces a location shift in the NLL distribution (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
32	
33	We extract seven distributional features per text, organized into two groups based on what they measure rather than how they are computed.
34	
35	\paragraph{Reference-model features.}
36	A held-out reference model (Pythia-410M, chosen to be smaller than and architecturally independent of all generators) computes per-token negative log-likelihood (NLL) for each text.
37	From the resulting NLL sequence, we extract five statistics:
38	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
39	    \item \textbf{entropy\_mean}: mean token-level NLL, capturing the average predictability of the text under the reference model;
40	    \item \textbf{entropy\_std}: standard deviation of token-level NLL, measuring the spread of per-token surprise;
41	    \item \textbf{entropy\_max}: maximum token-level NLL, capturing the most surprising token;
42	    \item \textbf{entropy\_min}: minimum token-level NLL, capturing the most predictable token---as generation depth increases, the floor of token-level surprise drops, reflecting the model's increasing confidence on its own outputs;
43	    \item \textbf{tail\_decay}: proportion of tokens whose NLL exceeds the 90th percentile of the reference distribution (computed over $\mathcal{C}_0$), measuring how heavy-tailed the NLL distribution is relative to human text.
44	\end{itemize}
45	
46	\paragraph{Surface features.}
47	Two features capture lexical diversity without requiring a reference model:
48	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
49	    \item \textbf{TTR}: type-token ratio (number of unique word types divided by total tokens);
50	    \item \textbf{hapax\_ratio}: proportion of words appearing exactly once (\emph{hapax legomena}).
51	\end{itemize}
52	
53	\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
54	The grouping reflects an empirical pattern we term \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features (entropy\_mean, TTR, hapax\_ratio) drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy\_std, tail\_decay) remain near-stationary.
55	This differential behavior---consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution while preserving its functional form---motivates combining both feature types.
56	As shown in \S\ref{sec:results}, the full 7-feature set significantly outperforms either group alone.
57	
58	\subsection{Evaluation Protocol}
59	\label{sec:evaluation}
60	
61	\paragraph{Cross-validation.}
62	To evaluate generalization to unseen generators, we use \textbf{Leave-One-Generator-Out (LOGO)} cross-validation: in each fold, one of the six generators is held out for testing and the remaining five provide training data.
63	We additionally report \textbf{Leave-One-Family-Out (LOFO)} results, where an entire model family (e.g., all Qwen models) is held out, testing generalization across architectural lineages.
64	
65	\paragraph{Classifier.}
66	We use XGBoost \cite{xgboost} as the classifier throughout.
67	Gradient-boosted trees handle heterogeneous feature scales and nonlinear interactions without extensive hyperparameter tuning, and their feature importance scores support interpretability.
68	We use $n\_\text{estimators}{=}200$, $\max\_\text{depth}{=}6$, and learning rate $0.1$ for the 7-feature ensemble.
69	Baseline detectors (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}) use the same XGBoost framework with $n\_\text{estimators}{=}100$ and $\max\_\text{depth}{=}3$ to avoid overfitting their single-feature input.
70	LOGO F1 is stable across random seeds (mean\,=\,0.789, std\,=\,0.0009 over 5 seeds), confirming that results are not sensitive to classifier initialization.
71	Alternative classifiers (random forest, logistic regression) yield comparable performance (Appendix~\ref{app:classifier}), confirming that discriminative power resides in the features, not the classifier.
72	
73	\paragraph{Metrics and statistical testing.}
74	The primary metric is \textbf{macro-averaged F1} over the three depth classes, which weights minority classes (gen-1, gen-2+) equally against the typically easier gen-0 class.
75	We report per-class F1 scores and 95\% bootstrap confidence intervals ($n{=}1{,}000$ resamples).
76	For pairwise model comparisons (e.g., full features vs.\ ablated subsets), we use the \textbf{McNemar test} on disagreement tables.
77	For comparisons against detection baselines, we use \textbf{paired bootstrap} significance tests.
78	All reported $p$-values are two-sided.
79	Feature--depth correlations (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) are computed on class-balanced subsamples (equal samples per depth class) to control for depth-class imbalance in the generation pipeline.
80	
81	\paragraph{Baselines.}
82	We compare the 7-feature ensemble against four single-score detection methods repurposed as ordinal depth predictors: Avg-LogProb, FastDetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt}, Binoculars \cite{binoculars}, and LD-Score \cite{ld_score}.
83	Each baseline score is used as a univariate feature in the same XGBoost framework under LOGO cross-validation, ensuring a controlled comparison.
84	
85	\paragraph{Length confound control.}
86	Since TTR and hapax\_ratio are mechanically length-dependent, we verify that depth signal is not an artifact of systematic length variation.
87	We conduct three complementary analyses: (1) Spearman correlation between text length and each feature (requiring $|\rho| < 0.15$ for non-confounded features), (2) classification with length-normalized features, and (3) comparison on length-matched subsets.
88

**结论**：depth signal 在排除 gen-0 后仍然显著（0.723 远超 chance 0.50）。Gen-0 的 99.4% 准确率确实有泄露贡献，但核心 depth discrimination 能力不依赖于此。7-feature 和 4-baseline+surface 基本持平。

- Pythia-1B F1：Pythia-410M ref = 0.856, OLMo ref = 0.845, Qwen ref = 0.848

% Abstract — Depth Fingerprinting of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
As LLM outputs accumulate on the web, training corpora increasingly contain recursively generated text of unknown provenance depth.
We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}---classifying text as human-written (gen-0), first-generation synthetic (gen-1), or deeper (gen-2+)---beyond binary detection.
We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features remain near-stationary.
A 7-feature ensemble exploiting this complementarity achieves leave-one-generator-out macro-F1 of 0.79 ($p < 0.001$ vs.\ all baselines) across 6 generators from 3 model families (0.6B--8.2B), with per-generator held-out F1 ranging from 0.68 to 0.86.
In our setting, depth-aware data curation does not outperform random subsampling, positioning depth fingerprinting as a diagnostic tool for provenance characterization rather than a curative tool for data selection.
\end{abstract}

1	\section{Results}
2	\label{sec:results}
3	
4	We evaluate depth fingerprinting along four axes: cross-generator classification (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}), differential depth response of individual features (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}), comparison with existing detection baselines (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), and downstream utility for data curation (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
5	
6	\subsection{Depth Classification Performance}
7	\label{sec:results-classification}
8	
9	Table~\ref{tab:logo-results} reports leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 for 3-class depth estimation (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) across six generators spanning three model families and parameter counts from 0.6B to 8.2B.
10	
11	The 7-feature ensemble achieves LOGO F1\,=\,0.789, significantly outperforming all individual detection baselines ($p<0.001$; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).
12	Per-generator held-out F1 ranges from 0.683 (Qwen3-8B) to 0.856 (Pythia-1B).
13	Per-class F1 varies by depth: gen-0\,=\,0.94, gen-2+\,=\,0.80, gen-1\,=\,0.64; the primary difficulty lies in distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, where feature margins narrow.
14	
15	\paragraph{Cross-scale transfer.}
16	The six-generator evaluation includes Qwen3-8B (8.2B parameters), confirming that depth signal persists at scales beyond the $\leq$2.8B training generators.
17	However, cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap: Qwen3-8B held-out F1\,=\,0.683 (CI [0.668, 0.694]), compared to 0.76--0.86 for $\leq$2.8B generators.
18	Text generated by larger models is more fluent, compressing feature margins and making depth distinctions harder.
19	Notably, adding Qwen3-8B data \emph{improves} classification on the original five generators (+1.1\,pp to 0.811), indicating that cross-scale diversity benefits rather than dilutes the training signal.
20	A volume-matched control confirms this gain is driven by generator diversity, not data quantity: upsampling the 4-generator training set to match the 5-generator count yields only +0.05\,pp, while the remaining +0.78\,pp (94\% of the total improvement) is attributable to the additional generator's distributional diversity.
21	We note that this gap may narrow with scale-matched training data; our current dataset contains $\sim$1{,}000 samples per generator regardless of scale.
22	
23	\paragraph{Cross-family generalization.}
24	Leave-one-family-out (LOFO) evaluation---holding out an entire model family and training on the remaining two---yields macro-F1 of 0.772 (Pythia held out), 0.762 (OLMo held out), and 0.754 (Qwen held out), confirming that depth features transfer across architectural families with only modest degradation (average $\Delta$\,=\,$-$2.6\,pp vs.\ LOGO).
25	
26	\paragraph{Length confound control.}
27	Text length correlates weakly with depth (Spearman $|\rho| < 0.14$).
28	Length-normalized feature trends are preserved, and length-matched subsampling yields comparable or higher F1 ($\Delta$\,=\,+0.041), ruling out length as a confound (Appendix~\ref{app:length}).

55	\label{sec:results-differential}
56	
57	Features exhibit \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity measures drift monotonically with depth, while distributional shape measures remain near-stationary.
58	This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution---the text becomes progressively more predictable (mean shifts), while the functional form of the distribution is preserved (shape is invariant).
59	
60	\begin{figure}[t]
61	\centering
62	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1_differential_response.pdf}
63	\caption{Differential depth response: Spearman correlations between individual features and generation depth. Central-tendency and diversity features (hapax ratio, TTR, entropy mean) show strong monotonic drift, while shape features (entropy std, tail decay) remain near-stationary.}

68	drifting features show strong monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.558$, TTR $\rho = -0.542$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.475$),

70

72	Table~\ref{tab:ablation} reports ablation results.
73	The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.789) significantly outperforms both surface-only features (TTR, hapax\_ratio; F1\,=\,0.729) and reference-only features (entropy mean/std/max/min, tail\_decay; F1\,=\,0.745; McNemar $p \approx 0$).
74	Permutation importance ranks hapax ratio highest (0.269), followed by entropy mean (0.164) and TTR (0.159).
75	Surface features capture vocabulary impoverishment; reference features capture distributional shift---neither subsumes the other.
76

78	To confirm that differential depth response is not an artifact of the Pythia-410M reference model, we compute features using three cross-family references: Pythia-410M, OLMo-2-1B, and Qwen3-0.6B.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

We evaluate depth fingerprinting along four axes: cross-generator classification (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}), differential depth response of individual features (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}), comparison with existing detection baselines (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), and downstream utility for data curation (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).

\subsection{Depth Classification Performance}
\label{sec:results-classification}

Table~\ref{tab:logo-results} reports leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 for 3-class depth estimation (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) across six generators spanning three model families and parameter counts from 0.6B to 8.2B.

The 7-feature ensemble achieves LOGO F1\,=\,0.789, significantly outperforming all individual detection baselines ($p<0.001$; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).
Per-generator held-out F1 ranges from 0.683 (Qwen3-8B) to 0.856 (Pythia-1B).
Per-class F1 varies by depth: gen-0\,=\,0.94, gen-2+\,=\,0.80, gen-1\,=\,0.64; the primary difficulty lies in distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, where feature margins narrow.

\paragraph{Cross-scale transfer.}
The six-generator evaluation includes Qwen3-8B (8.2B parameters), confirming that depth signal persists at scales beyond the $\leq$2.8B training generators.
However, cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap: Qwen3-8B held-out F1\,=\,0.683 (CI [0.668, 0.694]), compared to 0.76--0.86 for $\leq$2.8B generators.
Text generated by larger models is more fluent, compressing feature margins and making depth distinctions harder.
Notably, adding Qwen3-8B data \emph{improves} classification on the original five generators (+1.1\,pp to 0.811), indicating that cross-scale diversity benefits rather than dilutes the training signal.
A volume-matched control confirms this gain is driven by generator diversity, not data quantity: upsampling the 4-generator training set to match the 5-generator count yields only +0.05\,pp, while the remaining +0.78\,pp (94\% of the total improvement) is attributable to the additional generator's distributional diversity.
We note that this gap may narrow with scale-matched training data; our current dataset contains $\sim$1{,}000 samples per generator regardless of scale.

\paragraph{Cross-family generalization.}
Leave-one-family-out (LOFO) evaluation---holding out an entire model family and training on the remaining two---yields macro-F1 of 0.772 (Pythia held out), 0.762 (OLMo held out), and 0.754 (Qwen held out), confirming that depth features transfer across architectural families with only modest degradation (average $\Delta$\,=\,$-$2.6\,pp vs.\ LOGO).

\paragraph{Length confound control.}
Text length correlates weakly with depth (Spearman $|\rho| < 0.14$).
Length-normalized feature trends are preserved, and length-matched subsampling yields comparable or higher F1 ($\Delta$\,=\,+0.041), ruling out length as a confound (Appendix~\ref{app:length}).

\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{llccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Generator} & \textbf{Family} & \textbf{Params} & \textbf{Held-out F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
\midrule

Pythia-2.8B     & Pythia & 2.8B & 0.804 & [0.793, 0.813] \\

Qwen3-8B       & Qwen   & 8.2B & 0.683 & [0.668, 0.694] \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{l}{Average (6-gen LOGO)} & 0.789 & --- \\
\multicolumn{3}{l}{5-gen LOGO (excl.\ Qwen3-8B)} & 0.800 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Leave-one-generator-out macro-F1 with bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals ($n$\,=\,1000) for 3-class depth estimation using the 7-feature ensemble. Each row holds out one generator for testing and trains on the remaining five.}
\label{tab:logo-results}
\end{table}


\subsection{Differential Depth Response}
\label{sec:results-differential}

Features exhibit \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity measures drift monotonically with depth, while distributional shape measures remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution---the text becomes progressively more predictable (mean shifts), while the functional form of the distribution is preserved (shape is invariant).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1_differential_response.pdf}
\caption{Differential depth response: Spearman correlations between individual features and generation depth. Central-tendency and diversity features (hapax ratio, TTR, entropy mean) show strong monotonic drift, while shape features (entropy std, tail decay) remain near-stationary.}
\label{fig:feature-drift}
\end{figure}

Individual-level Spearman correlations with depth confirm the split (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}):
drifting features show strong monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.558$, TTR $\rho = -0.542$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.475$),
while shape features show weak or negligible correlations (entropy std $|\rho| = 0.076$, tail decay $|\rho| = 0.089$).

\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
Table~\ref{tab:ablation} reports ablation results.
The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.789) significantly outperforms both surface-only features (TTR, hapax\_ratio; F1\,=\,0.729) and reference-only features (entropy mean/std/max/min, tail\_decay; F1\,=\,0.745; McNemar $p \approx 0$).
Permutation importance ranks hapax ratio highest (0.269), followed by entropy mean (0.164) and TTR (0.159).
Surface features capture vocabulary impoverishment; reference features capture distributional shift---neither subsumes the other.

\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
To confirm that differential depth response is not an artifact of the Pythia-410M reference model, we compute features using three cross-family references: Pythia-410M, OLMo-2-1B, and Qwen3-0.6B.
All three achieve LOGO F1 between 0.80 and 0.82, with consistent drift directions across features.
The pattern generalizes across reference model architectures.

\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Feature set} & \textbf{LOGO F1} & \textbf{Top feature (importance)} \\
\midrule
Full (7 features)     & 0.789 & hapax\_ratio (0.269) \\
Surface only (2)      & 0.729 & hapax\_ratio (0.320) \\
Reference only (5)    & 0.745 & entropy\_mean (0.218) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Feature ablation (6-gen LOGO). Full $>$ surface = reference confirms complementarity between surface diversity features and reference-model distributional features.}
\label{tab:ablation}
\end{table}

Leave-one-feature-out analysis confirms that 6 of 7 features contribute positively, with entropy\_max showing the largest marginal impact despite modest split frequency (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}).


\subsection{Comparison with Detection Baselines}
\label{sec:results-baselines}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig3_baseline_comparison.png}
\caption{LOGO macro-F1 with 95\% bootstrap confidence intervals for each detection baseline and the 7-feature ensemble. Per-generator held-out F1 varies more for single detectors than for the ensemble.}
\label{fig:baseline-ci}
\end{figure}

We repurpose four existing detection scores as ordinal depth predictors by training the same ordinal classifier on each score as a single feature, using identical LOGO evaluation (Figure~\ref{fig:baseline-ci}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{LOGO F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textit{Multi-detector ensembles}} \\
4-det.\ + surface (6 feat.) & \textbf{0.805} & [0.800, 0.809] \\
4-detector ens.\ (4 feat.)  & 0.796 & [0.792, 0.801] \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textit{Single-model methods}} \\
7-feature ensemble    & \textbf{0.789} & [0.783, 0.792] \\
Avg-LogProb           & 0.737 & [0.732, 0.742] \\
FastDetectGPT         & 0.688 & [0.683, 0.693] \\
LD-Score              & 0.655 & [0.649, 0.660] \\
Binoculars            & 0.416 & [0.411, 0.422] \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Ordinal depth classification: all methods under unified 6-gen LOGO evaluation. The 7-feature ensemble outperforms all individual detection baselines; multi-detector ensembles achieve higher accuracy at the cost of running multiple detection pipelines.}
\label{tab:baselines}
\end{table}
The 7-feature ensemble outperforms every individual detection baseline: +5.2\,pp over Avg-LogProb ($p < 0.001$), +10.1\,pp over FastDetectGPT, +13.4\,pp over LD-Score, and +37.3\,pp over Binoculars (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).

The critical distinction is \emph{reliability}.
The ensemble achieves per-generator F1 ranging from 0.683 to 0.856 (std\,=\,0.058).
While this range reflects genuine difficulty variation across generators---particularly at larger scales (\S\ref{sec:results-classification})---the ensemble provides reliable performance even for the most challenging generator (Qwen3-8B: 0.683).
Each single detector captures partial depth signal---Avg-LogProb tracks mean perplexity shift, LD-Score captures character-level distributional change---but each fails on specific generator families.
The 7-feature ensemble aggregates complementary signals, producing stable performance regardless of the held-out generator.
The overall 95\% bootstrap CI [0.783, 0.792] reflects sampling precision of the pooled estimate, not cross-generator consistency.

\paragraph{Multi-detector ensembles.}
The multi-detector ensembles (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}) confirm that combining detection scores yields stronger depth signal.
Adding our surface features (TTR, hapax ratio) to the 4-detector ensemble further improves performance, confirming that surface diversity features capture signal complementary to detection scores.
However, multi-detector approaches require running multiple detection pipelines, while the 7-feature method uses a single lightweight reference model plus two vocabulary statistics.
The practical advantage of depth features lies in their interpretability---they reveal the differential depth response pattern (\S\ref{sec:results-differential})---and computational efficiency.
Baseline results are stable across classifier hyperparameters: using the ensemble's settings ($n\_\text{estimators}{=}200$, $\max\_\text{depth}{=}6$) instead of the default ($100$/$3$) changes baseline F1 by less than 0.002\,pp for all four detectors, confirming that performance differences reflect feature informativeness rather than classifier capacity.

\paragraph{Gen-0 data leakage control.}
Because gen-0 (human-written) seed texts are shared across all generators, LOGO evaluation creates a train--test overlap for the gen-0 class.
To verify that depth discrimination is not driven by this overlap, we evaluate all methods on a binary task (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) excluding gen-0 entirely (Table~\ref{tab:binary-logo}).
The 7-feature ensemble achieves binary LOGO F1\,=\,0.723, well above chance and consistent with the 3-class gen-1 and gen-2+ per-class F1 scores (0.64 and 0.80 respectively; \S\ref{sec:results-classification}).
The depth signal between gen-1 and gen-2+ is genuine and does not depend on the gen-0 overlap.

\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
\midrule
4-det.\ + surface   & 0.724 & [0.718, 0.730] \\
7-feature ensemble   & 0.723 & [0.717, 0.729] \\
Avg-LogProb          & 0.712 & [0.706, 0.719] \\
4-detector ens.\     & 0.712 & [0.705, 0.718] \\
LD-Score             & 0.701 & [0.694, 0.707] \\
FastDetectGPT        & 0.616 & [0.609, 0.622] \\
Binoculars           & 0.524 & [0.517, 0.531] \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Binary depth classification (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, gen-0 excluded) under 6-gen LOGO. Excluding gen-0 removes the shared-seed data overlap; depth discrimination remains significant.}
\label{tab:binary-logo}
\end{table}


\subsection{Downstream Utility: A Negative Finding}
\label{sec:results-downstream}

Can depth-aware data curation improve downstream language model quality?
We fine-tune OLMo-2-0425-1B on five data variants (3 seeds each) and evaluate perplexity on a held-out test set (Table~\ref{tab:downstream}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrc}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{Test PPL} \\
\midrule
All depths            & 12{,}299 & 2.335 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Size-matched (random) & 3{,}951  & 2.367 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0--1 only       & 3{,}951  & 2.387 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
Binary-filtered       & 3{,}951  & 2.389 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0 only          & 797      & 2.681 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Downstream fine-tuning perplexity (OLMo-2-0425-1B, mean $\pm$ std across 3 seeds). At equal sample count, random subsampling (2.367) outperforms depth-aware curation (depth 0--1: 2.387, binary-filtered: 2.389).}
\label{tab:downstream}
\end{table}

The results are unambiguous: data quantity dominates depth composition.
Training on all 12{,}299 samples yields the lowest perplexity (2.335).
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951), random subsampling (2.367) \emph{outperforms} both depth-stratified selection (depth 0--1: 2.387) and binary detection filtering (2.389).
Cross-seed variance is below 0.002 across all variants, confirming the robustness of this null result.

Restricting training to human-only text (depth 0, $n$\,=\,797) produces a sharp perplexity increase to 2.681, driven primarily by the 5$\times$ reduction in data volume rather than depth composition per se.

We report this negative finding transparently: depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data curation.
Knowing the generation depth of a document does not, by itself, make it more or less useful for training.
